standard.title: Significant Events and Turning Points of WWI
standard.description: significant events and turning points of the war and the nature of warfare, including the Western Front Battle of the Somme and the Armistice
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied the causes of WWI (AC9HH9K08) and the places and experiences of Australian soldiers (AC9HH9K09). They understand the geographic scope of the war and the nature of different theatres. This descriptor asks them to examine specific significant events and turning points — moving from description of conditions to analysis of historical significance.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate significant events and turning points of WWI, examine the nature of warfare, and evaluate the factors that ended the war.

nodes.label: A major battle in depth — locations, techniques and warfare
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate one major battle of WWI in depth, examining its locations, techniques, nature of warfare, and significance.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the key features of one major battle — its location, the scale of casualties, and the techniques used.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate one major battle (from: Gallipoli, Fromelles, the Somme, Pozières, Passchendaele, Bullecourt, Villers-Bretonneux, Beersheba) in depth — examining locations and terrain, tactical approaches, scale of casualties, new warfare techniques used, and significance for the broader war.
wider: Examine the Battle of Villers-Bretonneux from both Australian and German perspectives — using primary sources from both sides to assess how the same battle was experienced and narrated differently
Investigate the Gallipoli campaign as a strategic failure and a cultural triumph — examining how military defeat became the foundational event of Australian national identity

Examine the Battle of the Somme (1916) as an example of industrial-scale slaughter — analysing the planning decisions, the tactical failures, and the consequences for military thinking about offensive warfare
nodes.hinge_reason: A specific battle studied in depth provides the concrete historical knowledge that makes evaluation of turning points (Node 2) and the end of the war (Node 3) meaningful. Without detailed case knowledge, students cannot evaluate significance — they can only name events.

response_modes.reason: While one battle is studied in depth, exposure to multiple perspectives on that battle (enemy side, different unit types, different ranks) prevents a single-strand narrative and builds the analytical capacity needed for Node 2.

success_criteria: Investigates one major battle in sufficient depth to describe its location, techniques, scale, and significance
Examines at least two perspectives on that battle (e.g. perspectives of soldiers on opposing sides, or different unit types)

nodes.label: Multiple perspectives using primary sources
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine the perspectives of those who fought on both sides of the war using primary sources including diaries, letters, and newspapers.
nodes.minimum_width: Analyse one primary source (diary, letter, or newspaper) from the perspective of a person directly involved in WWI and explain what it reveals about their experience or view.
nodes.typical_width: Examine the perspectives of soldiers from both Allied and opposing sides using primary sources — comparing how the same events were experienced differently; use diaries, letters, and newspapers to construct a picture of how those involved understood the war's progress and meaning.
wider: Compare a soldier's private diary account with an official military communiqué about the same event — analysing the gap between private experience and public representation of the war
Examine wartime newspaper coverage and propaganda alongside private correspondence to assess how civilian and military understanding of the war differed
Investigate the use of censorship in WWI to examine how the perspectives available to us are already shaped by what authorities allowed to be communicated

response_modes.reason: Using sources from both sides — Allied and opposing — is important for developing genuine historical thinking about perspective. Students who only access Allied sources cannot interrogate the 'enemy' framing.

success_criteria: Analyses at least one primary source with identification of origin, purpose, and what it reveals about the perspective of the author
Compares at least two perspectives from different positions on the same event or aspect of the war

nodes.label: Turning points and end of the war
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate the significance of the Russian Revolution, American entry into the war, and the Armistice in ending the war.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two factors that contributed to the end of WWI and explain why they mattered.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate the significance of: the Russian Revolution (1917) and Russia's exit from the war; American entry (1917) and the infusion of fresh troops and resources; the German Spring Offensive and its failure; the Allied 100 Days Offensive; the Armistice of November 1918 — explaining how these factors interacted to produce the war's end.
wider: Evaluate the relative significance of the three turning points (Russian Revolution, American entry, Armistice) using a structured argument — assessing which had the greatest impact and what criteria are being used to judge significance
Examine the German domestic situation in late 1918 — mutinies, civilian unrest, economic collapse — to assess how internal collapse contributed to the Armistice alongside military factors
Investigate the Armistice negotiations and the terms imposed on Germany to connect the war's ending to the subsequent peace settlement and its contested legacy

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the full WWI knowledge sequence — requiring students to use their understanding of the war's causes, nature, and consequences to evaluate what ended it. Evaluation of significance is the endpoint of the descriptor.

success_criteria: Identifies and describes at least two factors contributing to the end of WWI
Evaluates the significance of at least one factor, explaining why it mattered for ending the war
